n: The scene becomes a courtroom. The Lord tells Micah to present His case, with the mountains and hills as the jury.
The mountains — ancient witnesses that have seen all of Israel’s history — are called to hear the Lord’s lawsuit against His people.
God speaks tenderly as the injured party: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Tell me!” His love is wounded, not merely His authority.

f.w: O my people, what have I done unto thee?

n: God reminds them of His saving acts: freeing them from slavery in Egypt and giving them leaders — Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

f.w: redeemed thee out of the house of servants

n: Remember how King Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God turned the curse into blessing — and how God brought them from Shittim across the Jordan to Gilgal. These memories show God’s faithfulness.
Now the people respond with questions: How should I come before God? With burnt offerings of the finest year-old calves?
The questions escalate absurdly: thousands of rams? Rivers of oil? Even my own firstborn child? People sometimes think they can buy God’s favor with outward offerings.

f.g: Child sacrifice was practiced by Israel’s neighbors and condemned by God (2 Kings 16:3).

n: Micah’s great answer: God has already shown what is good — act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. This summarizes true religion in one sentence.

f.w: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love and kindness.

n: The Lord calls out to Jerusalem. Wise people fear His name. Pay attention to the “rod” of discipline and to the One who sent it.
Are there still treasures gained by fraud in the houses of the wicked, and dishonest, short measures? God hates such cheating.

f.g: A shrunken ephah — a grain measure made smaller to cheat buyers.

n: Can God call people innocent who use rigged scales and bags of false weights? Honest business is a matter of holiness.
The city’s rich are violent and its people are liars.
So God will strike them and make them sick and desolate because of their sins.

f.w: make thee sick in smiting thee
f.g: Or “I have begun to strike you.”

n: They will eat but stay hungry; they’ll try to save things but fail, and what they save will be lost to war. These are covenant curses from the law of Moses.

f.w: Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied

n: They will sow but not harvest, press olives but not use the oil, make wine but not drink it.

f.w: Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap

n: They follow the wicked practices of Kings Omri and Ahab — the northern kings famous for Baal worship and injustice. So they will become a ruin, mocked by others.

f.g: An object of scorn — people whistle or hiss at it.
